structuredContent.body:
This PR adds a `lake-check` input that runs `lake check` (added in Lean `v4.35.0-rc1`): it builds the project, exports it, and replays the result through one or more kernels inside a bubblewrap sandbox, erroring on any use of a non-standard axiom. The reference manual places this among the other ways to validate a proof, in [Validating a Lean Proof](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs/#validating-comparator). `lake-check: "true"` uses Lean's own kernel; `"paranoid"` (`--paranoid`, added in `v4.35.0-rc2`) additionally runs every checker the toolchain bundles: `leanchecker-paranoid`, `lean4lean`, `nanoda`, `con-leche` and `con-ron`. Release toolchains ship all five, so nothing is cloned or compiled.

The script does not build the project itself. `lake check` builds it inside the sandbox, and whether it is also built on the runner first is the `build` input's business: leaving `build` on is faster, because `lake check` then starts from a populated `.lake`, while `build: false` keeps the project's code off the runner. Building unconditionally here would take that choice away.

Support is feature-detected from the content of `lake check --help` rather than from version strings, because toolchains are frequently nightlies or PR builds whose versions do not order usefully. A Lake without `lake check` prints its top-level help and still exits 0, so the detection cannot key off the exit status.

A requested check that cannot run is an error rather than a silent pass. The sandbox is probed before the check runs, because `lake check` exits 1 both when it rejects a project and when bubblewrap fails to start, and reporting a sandbox failure as a rejection would blame the project for a setup problem. The probe's own diagnostic picks the remedy the error names: a denied uid map means the runner restricts user namespaces, while a denied `pivot_root` means the job is running in a container and needs a privileged one.

Those two cases are the two runner families this was tested against. GitHub-hosted runners restrict user namespaces, so they need them granted before `lean-action` is called, which the README shows. Namespace runners fail differently, at `pivot_root`, for root as well as for the job user, and need `namespace-features:container.privileged=true` with the `-with-features` suffix on the machine label; such a container permits user namespaces too, so it needs nothing else. Automating the GitHub-hosted case is deliberately left to a follow-up, because it means running `sudo` to change a runner's security posture and deserves its own review.

Two functional tests, pinned to `v4.35.0-rc2`, cover this: `paranoid` on a privileged Namespace runner, asserting it passes on a clean package and fails once a `sorry` is introduced, and one asserting an unsupported toolchain fails loudly. The second pins the legacy toolchain rather than the moving default, so that it cannot quietly stop testing feature detection once the default gains `lake check`.

🤖 Prepared with Claude+Codex

structuredContent.body:
This PR adds a `lake-check-sandbox` input choosing how to make `lake check`'s bubblewrap sandbox able to start on a runner that will not otherwise permit it. It stacks on https://github.com/leanprover/lean-action/pull/190 — feat: add `lake-check` input for sandboxed independent kernel checks, and should be reviewed after it.

GitHub-hosted runners restrict the unprivileged user namespaces bubblewrap needs, so `lake-check` fails there until something grants them. Granting them means changing the runner, which `lean-action` will not do uninvited, so the input takes `"none"` (the default, change nothing), `"apparmor"`, `"sysctl"` or `"setuid"`. Whichever is chosen is applied only when the sandbox has been probed and found not to work, so a runner that already permits user namespaces is left untouched.

`"apparmor"` is the narrowest and the documented choice. Ubuntu's restriction denies unprivileged user namespaces to programs whose AppArmor profile does not grant `userns`, so a profile covering bubblewrap leaves the restriction in force for every other program, where `"sysctl"` relaxes it runner-wide and `"setuid"` leaves a setuid binary behind. Measured on `ubuntu-latest`: all three make the sandbox work, and under `"apparmor"` and `"setuid"` the sysctl stays at `1`.

Because these operations are privileged, they act only on a root-owned distribution bubblewrap at `/usr/bin/bwrap` or `/bin/bwrap`, never on a symlink, and never on an executable named by `COMPARATOR_BWRAP`. Without those guards, `PATH` or that variable would decide which file gets made setuid root or gains an AppArmor policy. Refusing a non-root owner also matters in its own right: `chmod u+s` on a file owned by the job user grants that user's privileges rather than root's, so it would leave the sandbox broken while appearing to have worked.

None of these changes is undone afterwards. The warnings and the documentation say so, because on a persistent self-hosted runner they outlive the job, and such runners are better configured once by their administrator with this left at `"none"`.

The sandbox probe now exercises the namespace and mount operations Lake itself uses rather than a bare bind, since a runner can permit `--ro-bind` and still refuse the sandbox Lake actually builds.

A functional test runs `paranoid` on `ubuntu-latest` under `"apparmor"`, so the option the documentation recommends is the one CI exercises.

🤖 Prepared with Claude+Codex

structuredContent.body:
This PR makes `nanoda: true` use the `leanexport` and `nanoda_bin` that recent release toolchains ship, instead of installing a Rust toolchain and building `lean4export` and `nanoda_lib` from source on every run. The bundled binaries are matched to each other and to the compiler that produced the `.olean` files, where the source path pinned `nanoda_lib` to a branch rather than a release. Toolchains that ship neither keep the existing path unchanged.

The permitted axioms are identical on both paths, so this changes what the step costs, not what it accepts.

It also deprecates `nanoda` and `nanoda-allow-sorry` in favour of `lake-check: paranoid`, which runs nanoda alongside every other bundled checker. One case has no migration, and the warning and the documentation say so rather than implying a clean swap: `lake check` permits only the standard axioms and cannot be told to tolerate `sorryAx`, so a project relying on `nanoda-allow-sorry: true` should stay on this input for now. `lake check --allow-sorry` would close that gap, and is worth requesting upstream.

Nothing here delegates `nanoda` to `lake check`. Doing so would widen the check from one kernel to five for someone who asked only for nanoda, and would change the axiom policy underneath projects that carry a `sorry`.

A functional test asserts both halves of the claim: that the check still passes on a toolchain bundling the binaries, and that no source build happened, since avoiding that is the point.

🤖 Prepared with Claude+Codex
